chunks: I asked him about a man who killed a man intentionally. So it was brought before the governor, and the governor handed him over to the guardians of the slain to let them kill him. Then a group of people leapt upon them and released the killer from the hands of the guardians.
So he said: I hold that those who released the killer from the hands of the guardians should be imprisoned until they produce the killer.
It was said: What if the killer dies while they are in prison? He said: If he dies, then upon them is the blood money (diyah), which they shall all pay collectively to the guardians of the slain.

key_terms.أَوْلِيَاءُ الْمَقْتُولِ: Guardians of the slain – the heirs who hold the right to demand qisas or accept diyah on behalf of the victim
key_terms.الدِّيَةُ: Diyah – blood money, a monetary compensation paid to the family of a victim when qisas cannot be executed
key_terms.الْقِصَاصُ: Qisas – retaliatory punishment equal to the offense (eye for an eye), obligatory in cases of intentional killing unless the heirs pardon or accept diyah
key_terms.الْوَالِي: Wali/governor – the civil authority responsible for administering legal judgments

ai.seo_question: What is the Islamic ruling on those who help a murderer escape from qisas?
ai.summary: Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq (AS) addresses a scenario where a convicted murderer is rescued by a third party during the execution of qisas (retaliatory justice). The Imam rules that those who intervened to free the killer must be imprisoned until they surrender him. If the killer dies during their imprisonment, they collectively bear responsibility for the diyah (blood money) owed to the victim's family. This ruling underscores the principle that obstructing the lawful execution of justice carries its own legal consequences.
